questions.title: Why does BLT need a separate entropy model for patching instead of learning boundaries end‑to‑end?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3 the authors train a small byte‑level language model and compute next‑byte entropies $H(x_i)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}} p_e(x_i\!=\!v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i})\log p_e(x_i\!=\!v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i})$ to decide where patches start. I would have expected the boundary predictor to be learned jointly with the main model (as in Nawrot et al., 2023). Could someone explain the practical reasons for keeping this step separate (e.g., computational cost, stability), and whether this introduces any bias or limits incremental patching at inference time?

questions.title: What exactly is meant by “incremental patching” and why does BPE fail this property?
questions.question_body: Section 3.5 defines incremental patching as $f_p(\mathbf{x}_{<i}) = f_p(\mathbf{x})_{<i}$. My confusion lies in why a standard BPE tokenizer does not satisfy this: if I feed a prefix "the " into BPE I get different tokenizations depending on whether I later add "cat" or "dog". How does BLT guarantee that its dynamic patches can be decided without seeing future bytes, especially when using entropy‑based thresholds that depend on context?

questions.title: How does the average patch size affect both training context length and inference FLOP budget?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that longer patches reduce inference FLOPs because the latent transformer runs fewer steps, yet they also adjust the byte sequence length so that the expected number of bytes per batch stays constant. Can someone clarify how changing average patch size $\bar{p}$ impacts (a) the effective context length seen by the global transformer and (b) the total FLOPs per byte as defined in Equation (2) in Section 4.3?

questions.title: Why are hash‑based n‑gram embeddings necessary and how do they differ from frequency‑based embeddings?
questions.question_body: Section 5.1 introduces hash $n$‑gram embeddings $E_{n}^{hash}(\text{Hash}(g_{i,n}))$ for $n=3\dots8$. I am not clear on why hashing is preferred over directly learning an embedding table for each possible n‑gram, especially given the claim that 500 K hash entries suffice. Also, what were the observed differences when using frequency‑based embeddings according to Appendix C?

questions.title: Can you explain the cross‑attention mechanism used in the encoder and decoder with an example?
questions.question_body: Both encoder and decoder contain cross‑attention blocks similar to Perceiver (Section 5.2). The description includes queries initialized by pooling bytes in a patch and keys/values coming from byte representations $h_{l,i}$. I'm unsure how these queries are constructed in practice (max‑pooling vs average pooling?) and how masking ensures each query only attends to its own patch bytes. A concrete step‑by‑step example with a simple three‑byte patch would help.

questions.title: How is Bits‑Per‑Byte (BPB) computed from cross‑entropy loss, and why is it preferred over perplexity for byte models?
questions.question_body: In Section 4.2 BPB is defined as $\text{BPB}(x)=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{CE}(\mathbf{x})}{\ln(2) \cdot n_{\text{bytes}}}$. I understand this normalizes cross‑entropy by number of bytes, but I'm unclear about the conversion factor $\ln(2)$. Is this simply converting nats to bits? Also, does BPB allow direct comparison between tokenized LLMs (with different vocabulary sizes) and byte LLMs?

questions.title: What are the theoretical FLOP savings from using block‑causal attention in the global transformer versus standard causal attention?
questions.question_body: The global transformer uses a block‑causal mask as per Dubey et al., 2024. How does this differ from ordinary causal masking in terms of computational complexity per layer? Does it impact model capacity or only speed up inference when processing long sequences of patches?

questions.title: Why does space‑patching perform almost as well as entropy‑patching despite being a simple heuristic?
questions.(question_body): "Space patching" creates a new patch after any whitespace-like byte (Section 3.2). The results in Figure 4 show it close to entropy patching on scaling curves. Is there an intuition why word boundaries already capture most high‑entropy points? Are there data domains where space‐patching noticeably underperforms entropy‐based methods?

questions.title: How do they ensure that dynamic patches do not lead to excessively long sequences causing memory spikes during training?
questions.(question_body): "During training we pad and possibly truncate byte sequences to 12k and 24k bytes respectively for Llama 2 and BLT‑1T datasets" (Section 4.4). Could someone elaborate on how the maximum allowed patch size is enforced, e.g., by clipping entropy thresholds or discarding outlier patches? How often do such truncations happen in practice?

questions.title: What is the impact of increasing n‑gram hash table size beyond 500 K entries on model performance?
questions.(question_body): "Going from 300 K to 500 K hashes changed performance by ~0.001 BPB at 8B scale" (Section 6). Does this suggest diminishing returns after a certain point, or could larger tables become beneficial if combined with more layers in the local encoder? Are there memory or latency concerns with larger hash tables?

questions.title: "Fixed inference flop scaling" shows BLT crossing token models earlier at larger FLOP budgets – what drives this crossing point?
questions.(question_body): "The crossover point shifts from 3× compute-optimal budget down to 2.5×" (Section 5.4). Is this primarily due to reduced proportion of FLOPs spent on local encoder/decoder as model size grows, or because larger patches provide better long‑range context per compute unit? How would you expect this trend to continue beyond 8B parameters?

questions.(title): "How does BLT achieve robustness to character‐level noise compared to tokenizer models?")
questions.(question_body): "BLT outperforms Llama 3 on noised HellaSwag by ~8 points" (Section 7). Is this robustness solely due to operating on raw bytes, or do hash n‑gram embeddings and dynamic patching also contribute? Has any ablation isolated which component gives the biggest gain against specific corruptions like random case changes or character drops?
